extracted.intended_audience: citizens, legislators, and political observers concerned with the constitution and conduct of the House of Commons (English public/political class)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for judging the proper constitution, spirit, and conduct of the House of Commons: its relation to the people, limits on its powers, duties toward public money, and signs of corruption or perversion. Focused on normative standards for representation and parliamentary behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular origin and transitory nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons was supposed originally to be 'no part of the standing government of this country' and considered as a 'control issuing immediately from the people' and 'speedily to be resolved into the mass from whence it arose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the Commons retains a transitory, non-permanent character tied to the people (e.g., regular elections and sensitivity to public feeling) rather than acting as a permanent magistracy. Anti-pattern: the Commons becoming a 'standing senate' detached from constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commons as 'express image' of the nation's feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: The virtue, spirit, and essence of a House of Commons consists in its being 'the express image of the feelings of the nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the assembly reflects popular opinion and feeling in practice (not merely formal derivation). Signs of failure: no sympathy with public opinion; acting in harmony with ministers whom the people abhor.

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Commons is a control 'for' the people, not 'upon' them
rubrics_metrics.description: It was not instituted to be a control 'upon' the people, as of late it has been taught; it was designed as a control 'for' the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether Commons' actions check executive/judicial power and protect popular interests, rather than suppressing or penalizing popular expression. Anti-pattern: using parliamentary power to punish popular qualities or to suppress complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core functions: vigilance over magistracy, public money, openness to complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: A vigilant and jealous eye over executory and judicial magistracy; an anxious care of public money; an openness, approaching towards facility, to public complaint: these seem to be the true characteristics of a House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure performance against these practical duties: oversight of executive/judicial actions, rigorous stewardship of public funds, and accessible handling of public grievances. Examples in text show neglect of these duties when Parliament pays before demanding accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of indiscriminate ministerial support
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule of indiscriminate support to all ministers... destroys the very end of Parliament as a control, and is a general, previous sanction to misgovernment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag as corrupt when the Commons routinely backs ministers without scrutiny. Evaluate whether parliamentary majority acts as an automatic sanction for executive misdeeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of free election rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting up any claims adverse to the right of free election; for this tends to subvert the legal authority by which the House of Commons sits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether mechanisms or precedents are being created that undermine free elections (e.g., discretionary incapacitation, substitution of members not chosen by electors). Anti-pattern: altering right of election to disable disagreeable persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent recourse and reasonable duration of Parliaments
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliaments must therefore sit every year, and for great part of the year... the constant habit of authority, and the unfrequency of elections, have tended very much to draw the House of Commons towards the character of a standing senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the timing and duration of sessions maintain connection with the electorate. Long gaps or lengthy terms that reduce electoral responsiveness are negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of delegation-to-original-power shift (corruption of principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: This change from an immediate state of procuration and delegation to a course of acting as from original power, is the way in which all the popular magistracies in the world have been perverted from their purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether representatives act as trustees deriving authority from the people or behave as if they possess original, independent authority. The latter signals systemic corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament must not assume executive functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If they have any evil design to which there is no ordinary legal power commensurate, they bring it into Parliament. In Parliament the whole is executed from the beginning to the end... Parliament cannot, with any great propriety, punish others for things in which they themselves have been accomplices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether legislative bodies are being used to perform executive acts without proper checks — a sign of lost control and accountability. Example: using Parliament to execute ministerial designs shields them from legal reckoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment and guardian institutions endangered by parliamentary complicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Impeachment, that great guardian of the purity of the constitution, is in danger of being lost, even to the idea of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether Parliament's participation in executive acts undermines other constitutional safeguards (impeachment, judicial review). Loss of those functions diminishes corrective mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition and popularity must not be penalized by discretionary legislative sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whilst any errors committed in support of power were left to the law... all excesses on the side of liberty... were not only to be punished by the rigor of the known law, but by a 'discretionary' proceeding, which brought on 'the loss of the popular object itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fairness of consequences for popular dissent versus servility: practices that make popularity a ground for disqualification (but not servility) are perverse and suppress representative duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elections must reflect actual, bona fide choice of electors
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of election was not established merely as a 'matter of form'... It is a right, the effect of which is to give to the people that man, and 'that man only', whom, by their voices actually, not constructively given, they declare that they know, esteem, love, and trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that elected members are the specific persons chosen by electors, not legal fictions or substitutes. Anti-pattern: treating election as formality or substituting 'shadows' (fictive replacements) for true choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative bodies must not act as 'courts of criminal equity'
rubrics_metrics.description: A committee of council, or a House of Commons, or a House of Lords; the liberty of the subject will be equally subverted by it. A large and liberal construction in ascertaining offences, and a discretionary power in punishing them, is the idea of 'criminal equity'; which is in truth a monster in jurisprudence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject practices where legislature creates vague offences and applies discretionary punishments outside regular legal procedures. Such legislative criminal equity subverts liberty and due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: No arbitrary discretionary rule in exercising disqualification power
rubrics_metrics.description: The power which they claim, of declaring incapacities, would not be above the just claims of a final judicature, if they had not laid it down as a leading principle, that they had no rule in the exercise of this claim, but their own 'discretion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require explicit principles, modes of proceeding, standards of evidence and limits when removing members. A power exercised solely by 'occasional will' is unlawful and constitutionally dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of law: Parliament should not 'declare' law by occasional will
rubrics_metrics.description: We do not 'make' laws. No; we do not contend for this power. We only 'declare' law; and as we are a tribunal both competent and supreme, what we declare to be law becomes law... the judgment does not derive its validity from its conformity to the law; but preposterously the law is made to attend on the judgment; and the rule of the judgment is no other than the 'occasional will of the House.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate conformity to rule-of-law principles: legal determinations should follow established law and procedure, not be retrofitted to justify parliamentary judgments. Anti-pattern: letting judgments define law post hoc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary stewardship of public money: accounts must precede payment
rubrics_metrics.description: The capital use of an account is, that the reality of the charge... should all appear antecedent to the payment. No man ever pays first, and calls for his account afterwards... In national business, there is an additional reason for a previous production of every account. It is a check... upon a corrupt and prodigal use of public money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether Parliament demands detailed accounts before authorizing payment (prevention) rather than paying first and auditing later (which invites misapplication and collusion). Example negative practice: 'payment previous to account' made a settled rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage, honors, and civil_list dependence corrupt parliamentary independence
rubrics_metrics.description: On the side of the court will be, all honors, offices, emoluments; every sort of personal gratification... To complete the scheme... it was necessary, in effect, to destroy those appropriations of revenue, which seem to limit the property, as the other laws had done the powers, of the crown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for systemic incentives (offices, pensions, grants, civil list debts) that bind members to the crown or ministers. Unlimited funds or mortgaging revenue to the crown creates dependence and subverts representative duty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituents must retain effective control over representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Commons can never be a control on other parts of government, unless they are controlled themselves by their constituents; and unless those constituents possess some right in the choice of that House, which it is not in the power of that House to take away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure whether mechanisms exist for constituents to influence, recall, or otherwise hold representatives accountable; absent such control, representative duty cannot be faithfully performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and investigation of misuse of public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Would it not have been natural for Parliament first to have asked how, and by what means, their appropriated allowance came to be insufficient?... To put their hands upon such articles of expenditure as they thought improper or excessive, and to secure, in future, against such misapplication or exceeding?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether Parliament proactively investigates causes of deficits and maladministration, seeks to identify culpable officials, and reforms appropriations to prevent recurrence. Passive acceptance or postponement of inquiry is a failing.
